source.title: Transformers for dynamical systems learn transfer operators in-context
source.authors: Anthony Bao; Jeffrey Lai; William Gilpin

record.tranche_reason: It measures held-out loss during training and reports epoch-wise double descent, using the same training-time sweep and test-loss measurement as the original claim in a new model and task setting.
record.gate_note: The paper cites prior double-descent work, but those cited results are not rows. Results about context-length scaling, attractor dimensions, and transfer-operator estimation do not test the other claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study tracks held-out cross-entropy over training epochs and reports epoch-wise double descent (V2). The setting is new: a two-layer, single-head transformer forecasting tokenized dynamical-system time series. It differs from the originals' image-classification setups, which used label noise, so this is T3 rather than T1.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate for the double-descent part. However, the paper's main conclusions concern mechanism: transformers perform in-context time-delay embedding and estimate transfer (Perron-Frobenius) operators to forecast unseen systems. Double descent is a secondary observation.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures held-out cross-entropy across training in a compact transformer forecasting dynamical systems, rather than reproducing the original model and task settings; it also reports separate in-distribution and out-of-distribution curves.
record.method_sensitivity: The appendix reports that the epoch-wise double-descent phenomenon becomes more pronounced with longer context lengths.
record.problems: The evidence concerns a compact two-layer transformer trained on a single dynamical system per experiment. The loss-curve values are presented in figures rather than numerical text; the reported uncertainty is standard error across 100 replicate system pairs.
record.rows_left_out: No other results bearing on the tested claim version were omitted.

untested.parts: Not tested: other architectures and tasks; dependence on label noise or regularization (weight decay is fixed at 0, there is no label noise); peak location relative to the interpolation point.
Training sample size is not varied.
No capacity sweep across model classes.
No effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location. The authors note only that longer context makes the effect more pronounced, 'consistent with' increasing complexity.
Label noise and regularization are not varied, and multiple peaks are not examined.
Complexity is not recounted with an effective number of parameters.

record.verdict_notes: Epoch-wise double descent appears here without injected label noise or weight decay, in deterministic chaotic-trajectory data. All double-descent evidence is figure-only, with no peak epochs or loss values stated in the text. Neither original source is this study, so the verdicts apply.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test whether epoch-wise double descent holds across other model families or training tasks.
Training sample size is not swept near an interpolation threshold.
The study does not test capacity scaling across model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location.
The study does not test label-noise or regularization dependence, multiple descent peaks, or disappearance under optimally tuned regularization.
The study does not recount complexity using an effective parameter measure.
